title: Coral and the Visitor
premise: August Delacroix, a folklorist and reluctant heir to their grandmother's salt-marsh house, has spent twenty years rationalizing the sounds in the walls—until every mirror in the house begins reflecting the room exactly one second late, and the reflection starts moving first. The lag is a count: each night it lengthens by one second, and on the harvest moon, when the lag reaches the length of a life, whatever has been waiting in the glass will step out to collect the debt their grandmother incurred by trading a neighbor's child for her family's survival. August must gather the scattered Delacroix relatives, lead them through the village's forbidden song—the one no one will sing twice—to the old mirror-well, and shatter the inheritance before the count completes, knowing the price is that someone must stay behind in the glass. In the end August sends the family ahead, sings the song a second time alone, and trades their own reflection for the child's freedom, surviving as a person the mirrors no longer show.
about_author: M. M. Vasquez is the pen name of a former archivist of Gulf Coast oral histories who grew up in a family that refused to discuss its own past. Their fiction explores debts that outlive the people who incurred them.

chapters.title: The Second Behind the Glass
chapters.summary: August, POV, cataloging the house's sounds for the last time before selling it, notices the bathroom mirror lagging—one second, then two. They test every mirror with a metronome and a candle, telling themselves it's a trick of old silvering. The beat is the vertigo of a rationalist watching their explanations fail in real time.

chapters.title: Songs Nobody Sings Twice
chapters.summary: Still August's POV, they interview the village's last three elders about the harvest song for their folklore archive. Each refuses on the second verse; one, old Thérèse, grabs August's wrist and says the lag has started early this generation. The beat is dread refracted through politeness—a community's complicity dressed as hospitality.

chapters.title: What Grandmother Traded
chapters.summary: In the attic, August finds the ledger: their grandmother's debts recorded not in money but in names, the last entry a neighbor's child, Émile, taken the winter of the flood. The mirror in the ledger's glassine sleeve reflects August before they enter the frame. The beat is the sick recognition that inheritance is a contract, not a gift.

chapters.title: The Family That Scattered
chapters.summary: August calls the estranged Delacroix cousins—POV shifts briefly to cousin Rosalie in Baton Rouge, who hangs up, then to teenage Theo, who has been dreaming in a reflection that isn't his. August realizes the lag is reaching all of them. The beat is the loneliness of being the only one willing to look.

chapters.title: Five Seconds
chapters.summary: Back in the house, the lag reaches five seconds; August watches their reflection finish pouring coffee they haven't poured yet, and it smiles first. Thérèse dies that night with the song half-sung, her mouth still moving in her bedroom mirror. The beat is grief weaponized—the count does not wait for mourning.

chapters.title: The Well Under the Floorboards
chapters.summary: Following the ledger's map, August tears up the kitchen floor and finds the mirror-well: a shaft lined with glass, holding every reflection the family ever surrendered, including a small boy who still waits at the bottom. The lag jumps to nine seconds. The beat is horror curdling into resolve—witnessing makes rescue possible.

chapters.title: Gathering the Count
chapters.summary: August herds the reluctant cousins back to the house as the harvest moon waxes; Rosalie arrives furious, Theo arrives already half-transparent in photographs. The family reads the ledger aloud and each must name what their comfort cost. The beat is the painful assembly of justice outside any court—accountability as ritual.

chapters.title: The First Verse, Sung Twice
chapters.summary: On the penultimate night the family sings the forbidden song together, and the house answers—walls of glass, reflections stepping a full ten seconds ahead, herding them toward the well. Theo nearly walks into the shaft; Rosalie pulls him back and finally believes. The beat is terror becoming solidarity.

chapters.title: The Harvest Moon
chapters.summary: Climax, August's POV: under the full moon the lag completes, and the thing wearing their grandmother's face rises from the well to collect. August sends the family out the back road, then sings the second verse alone, offering their own reflection as payment for Émile's release. The beat is sacrifice chosen freely at last.

chapters.title: A House With No Mirrors
chapters.summary: Resolution, Rosalie's POV: the mirrors are gone, the well is filled with salt, and Émile's name is finally spoken at a real grave. August lives on at the marsh edge, unphotographable, teaching the village the song openly. The beat is quiet, earned peace—the price of survival paid, and worth it.
